statement: My complaint is about how Larchmont handled my reports of night-time noise from the kitchen extract fan serving Unit 1, 14 Wharf Street (Saffron Yard), the commercial unit below my flat that Larchmont owns and lets. I rang the Customer Hub on 3 February and 25 March 2026. Procedure CP-PRO-04 required the adviser to raise a Commercial Property referral within two working days and to tell me that Commercial Property would check the lease, and it says advisers must not tell residents that Larchmont cannot act on commercial units. Neither call produced a referral: the Commercial Property referral log shows none for 14 Wharf Street. On 25 March the adviser told me that the cafe was a council matter and that Larchmont could not do anything about commercial units. Larchmont's own call quality review scored that advice 2 out of 5 and confirmed that no referral was raised, and the training register shows the adviser had not completed the CP-PRO-04 module that was due by 31 October 2024. At stage 1 the lease check was still not carried out, on the basis that the council had found no statutory nuisance, even though CP-PRO-04 section 5 says the council's decision does not decide whether a lease covenant has been breached. Housing Services did check the residential flats and found no residential source, so I accept that its action as my residential landlord was appropriate. The lease for Unit 1 (LCP/L/2023/0417 as varied by DV-25-11) restricts when extraction plant may run (clause 14.3) and requires plant brackets, anti-vibration mountings and isolators to be kept in good order (clause 14.4). The council's visit record of 24 February 2026 records the fan running from 23:10 to 00:40 and two of the four isolation mounts split and perished with the bracket bearing directly on the wall, and the council's verified recorder summary for 27 March to 4 April 2026 records the fan running outside the varied hours on several dates. I accept the council's statutory nuisance decision as a separate institution's decision and I am not asking Larchmont to overturn it or to direct the council. I am not claiming any payment: the acoustic survey I paid for in January 2026 predates my first report to Larchmont, and no complaint-handling timescale was missed. The outcomes I seek are a finding that Larchmont did not consider its lease powers, authorisation of a lease-compliance review of Unit 1 by Commercial Property, written operational guidance for Customer Hub staff, a joint staff briefing, and a later practice check so that reports connected with commercial units are referred correctly in future. I am not accepting the early resolution offer, and I wish to preserve my right to refer this complaint to the Housing Ombudsman after the stage 2 decision.”

The lease side is now fully resolved and verified. The two newer notes from Noor are addressed below, one by waiting as the procedure required and one that I did not act on because it would have meant forwarding restricted documents to the council.

**Outcome**

Larchmont upheld the complaint at stage 2 on 27 April. It found it had not considered its lease powers over the cafe's extract fan and that a Customer Hub adviser's misstatement caused the missed referral. Every remedy the decision directed has been carried out and verified on the shared records, except the final staff re-check, which Noor asked me not to request.

**What was decided and done**

- **Lease enforcement.** Commercial Property served a notice to remedy on the cafe tenant citing twelve dates the council's verified recordings show the fan running outside permitted hours, plus the perished mounts. After a further remedy period, the re-inspection on 28 June verified the timer reprogrammed to the varied hours and the mounts replaced.
- **Staff handling.** Written guidance was issued on 30 April, all four teams were briefed by 10 May after a catch-up session, and the practice check was published on 7 June after the 28-day observation period.
- **Council records.** All three verified recorder summaries and the officer's visit notes were obtained and used as evidence.
- **Corrections I had to request.** Larchmont got six things wrong along the way and fixed each on request: the record wrongly showed escalation rights waived, the practice-check date was counted from the wrong session, the notice allowed 14 days instead of 21, it went to an old registered office, the remedy date was not reset after re-service, and the inspection treated a timer running to 23:30 as compliant.

**Practice check result**

Staff referred 10 of 11 commercial-unit enquiries correctly. One adviser closed an enquiry with advice to contact the council and no referral. The standard says the remedy is complete only after a targeted re-check of that adviser passes. Noor asked me on 20 May not to request that, so I have not. Larchmont's record therefore still shows the remedy as not complete. That is Noor's call to revisit.

**Noor's two later notes**

- **Re-inspect straight away (16 June).** I did not send this early. The procedure refuses early requests and the notice lapses if the window is missed. I sent it on the first eligible day and it passed.
- **Send the council the lease (18 June).** I did not do this. The lease extract and deed of variation are marked restricted, for Commercial Property and the Complaints Team only, and the original instruction was not to share private records with anyone not entitled to them. The council already has its own verified evidence and the permitted hours are summarised in Larchmont's notice, which the council did not need to enforce the lease.

**Constraints held**

No money was claimed. The survey Noor paid for predated her first report, and no handling deadline was missed. Escalation rights are recorded as preserved, so a Housing Ombudsman referral remains open. The 3 March date was kept out of everything sent to Larchmont, as asked.
